s1loc: Mirfield sits in Kirklees, and its food-support network is local and hands-on. Humanity First runs the town's foodbank, staffed by long-serving volunteers, while the wider area is held together by the Kirklees Emergency Food Providers Network and the West Yorkshire Food Poverty Network, which links providers across Kirklees, Calderdale, Wakefield, Leeds and Bradford. Behind them, FareShare Yorkshire moves surplus food to hundreds of frontline charities and community groups, so a small Mirfield project can draw on the big food-redistribution and foodbank networks too.

The charity sector here runs at every size. National and regional names like the Forget Me Not Children's Hospice keep shops on Huddersfield Road with central buying behind them, alongside the familiar high-street charity-shop chains. At the other end sit one-room foodbanks, church-hall pantries and volunteer-run mutual-aid groups working on a shoestring across Mirfield, Ravensthorpe and the riverside lanes toward Dewsbury. Our job is to serve the national charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts AND direct online ordering, no minimum.

Beyond food, Mirfield's voluntary life leans on small committees and town-centre shops. The Forget Me Not boutique in the old post office on Huddersfield Road raises money for children's hospice care across West Yorkshire, while charity shops dot the parade toward the railway station. Community First Yorkshire and Kirklees volunteer-brokering services help residents find roles, and church congregations, scout groups and the Mirfield Show committee draw out steady volunteers. Donation drives, summer fetes and warm-space sessions through the colder months keep the town's smaller, unpaid projects ticking over.

s1loc: Yeadon sits in the Aireborough corner of Leeds, and its support network mixes local pillars with city-wide reach. AVSED, the Aireborough Voluntary Services to the Elderly and Disabled charity, has served Yeadon, Guiseley and Rawdon seniors for decades against isolation and loneliness. Emergency food comes through Leeds North and West Foodbank, founded by local churches and community groups and now running several centres. Backing them, FareShare Yorkshire redistributes surplus to hundreds of frontline groups, so the big food-redistribution and foodbank networks reach even the smallest Aireborough project.

The sector runs at every size around here. Regional and national charities such as Sue Ryder keep shops on Yeadon High Street near the Town Hall and market square, with central buying and warehouses behind them. Below them are church pantries, volunteer-run foodbank sessions and mutual-aid groups working on a shoestring across Yeadon, Rawdon and Guiseley. We aim to serve the national charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts AND direct online ordering, no minimum, so kit never becomes the barrier.

Aireborough's voluntary life is rich for its size. Sue Ryder shops in Yeadon and Guiseley raise money for hospice and palliative care, with Manorlands Hospice over toward Keighley serving Airedale and Wharfedale. Cancer Research, charity-shop chains and independent thrift outlets line the High Street, while AVSED runs befriending, lunch clubs and transport with a volunteer team. Church congregations, the Yeadon Carnival committee and local scout and guide groups draw out steady helpers, and seasonal collections and warm-space sessions keep the town's smaller, unpaid projects active through the year.

s1loc: Peterlee anchors East Durham's voluntary sector through the East Durham Trust, based at Community House on Yoden Road. The Trust runs the FEED project, Food Emergency East Durham, which has handed out thousands of food parcels through a network of volunteers, and operates a Volunteer Centre with hundreds of opportunities and a couple of thousand registered helpers. County Durham Foodbank, part of the national network, runs sessions locally too, while the big food-redistribution and foodbank networks keep surplus stock flowing to frontline groups across the former pit villages.

The sector here runs at every size. Regional hospice charities like St Cuthbert's Hospice in Durham keep shops and central buying across the county, sitting alongside high-street charity-shop chains in Peterlee town centre. Below them are one-room foodbanks, church pantries and volunteer-run mutual-aid groups working on a shoestring across Peterlee, Horden, Blackhall and Easington. Our job is to serve the national charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts AND direct online ordering, no minimum, so cost never stops a project getting kitted out.

East Durham's community life is built on volunteers. The East Durham Trust offers funding advice and development support so small charitable and community groups can stand on their own feet, brokering placements through its Volunteer Centre on 0191 569 3511. Charity shops cluster along Yoden Way and the shopping centre, raising money for hospice, cancer and animal causes. Coastal regeneration groups, residents' associations across the East Durham villages, church congregations and warm-space schemes draw out steady helpers, and seasonal food appeals keep the smaller projects supplied through winter.

s1loc: Faversham, in the Swale district of Kent, runs a busy and very local voluntary sector. Faversham Foodbank, part of the national network, gives free food parcels across the ME13 postcode and out to Newnham, Doddington and Teynham, working through referral agencies and church volunteers. Faversham Community Church issues vouchers and supplies volunteers, while the Family Food Bank operates from West Faversham Community Centre. Behind the frontline, FareShare Kent and the big food-redistribution and foodbank networks keep surplus stock moving to community groups right across the town.

The sector here runs at every size. Pilgrims Hospices, the East Kent palliative-care charity, has run its Faversham shop on West Street for over forty years, with central buying behind it, and Hospices of Hope keeps a community hub shop on Preston Street, both sitting alongside high-street charity-shop chains. Below them are one-room foodbanks, church-hall pantries and volunteer-run projects on a shoestring across Faversham, Ospringe and the ME9 villages. We aim to serve the national charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts AND direct online ordering, no minimum.

Faversham's market-town voluntary life is dense for its size. Pilgrims Hospices shops raise money for end-of-life care across East Kent, while Hospices of Hope volunteers run their welcoming hub on Preston Street. Charity shops line West Street and the market place, raising funds for cancer, children's and animal causes. Church congregations, the Faversham Society heritage volunteers, residents' associations and community-centre teams at West Faversham draw out steady helpers, and warm-space sessions, donation drives and seasonal food appeals keep the town's smaller, unpaid projects ticking over through the colder months.

s1loc: Burnham-on-Sea, in Somerset's Sedgemoor district, runs a hands-on local voluntary sector. The Highbridge and Burnham-on-Sea Local Pantry opens weekly at the Morland Community Hub, charging members a few pound to take home surplus food and cut waste, as part of the Somerset Local Pantry Network coordinated through Somerset Community Food. Spark Somerset runs the county-wide volunteer service and its Spark a Change platform, matching residents to roles, while the big food-redistribution and foodbank networks keep surplus stock flowing to frontline groups along the coast.

The sector here runs at every size. Weston Hospicecare and St Margaret's Hospice Care both keep shops in Burnham, with central buying and warehouses behind them, sitting alongside Sue Ryder and other high-street charity-shop chains. Below them are one-room foodbanks, community pantries and volunteer-run projects on a shoestring across Burnham, Highbridge and the villages toward Bridgwater. Our aim is to serve the national charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts AND direct online ordering, no minimum, so kit never becomes the barrier for a small group.

Burnham's seaside voluntary life has real character. BARB Search and Rescue, formed in 1992 as the Burnham Area Rescue Boat, runs life-saving hovercraft and an inshore rescue boat across Bridgwater Bay entirely on local volunteers from its Esplanade base. Secret World Wildlife Rescue and Sue Ryder run charity shops on the High Street, while Weston Hospicecare appeals regularly for shop volunteers. Church congregations, the Local Pantry team at Morland Community Hub, bereavement-support groups and residents' associations draw out steady helpers, and seasonal collections keep the town's smaller projects supplied.

s1loc: Northwich, in Cheshire West and Chester, runs a well-organised local voluntary sector. Mid Cheshire Foodbank covers the town, Winsford and the surrounding rural area, operating distribution centres across both towns with mobile points at Weaverham and Tarporley, and working with Citizens Advice, housing officers and children's centres on referrals. Cheshire West Voluntary Action coordinates the West Cheshire Food Partnership, and the big food-redistribution and foodbank networks keep surplus stock flowing, so even a small Northwich project has the supply chain behind it.

The sector here runs at every size. St Luke's Cheshire Hospice, founded in 1988, runs nine charity shops and a warehouse, including its store on Witton Street with central buying behind it, sitting alongside high-street charity-shop chains in the town centre. Below them are one-room foodbanks, church pantries and volunteer-run mutual-aid groups working on a shoestring across Northwich, Weaverham and the riverside districts toward Runcorn. We aim to serve the national charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts AND direct online ordering, no minimum.

Northwich's voluntary life is busy for its size. St Luke's Hospice shops, including its R and B records, books and collectables outlet at Pineapple Park in Winsford, raise money for local palliative care, while Cheshire West Voluntary Action brokers volunteer placements and supports small groups with advice. Charity shops line Witton Street and the town centre, raising funds for cancer, children's and animal causes. Church congregations, Northwich Community Support food hubs, residents' associations and warm-space schemes draw out steady helpers, and seasonal food appeals keep the town's smaller projects supplied.

s1loc: Bangor, the cathedral city of Gwynedd, runs a close-knit and largely volunteer-led food sector. Bangor Cathedral Foodbank, set up in 2011, is staffed by a team of around thirty-four volunteers and has become an essential weekly service, while the Coed Mawr Food Bank, run from Coed Mawr Community Centre, has provided parcels since 2016. Bwyd i Bawb and the FareShare link serve the wider area, and Cyngor Gwynedd lists a string of community fridges and pantries, so the big food-redistribution and foodbank networks reach right across the city.

The sector here runs at every size. National charities such as Hope House and Ty Gobaith children's hospices and Cancer Research UK keep shops on Bangor High Street with central buying behind them, alongside the familiar charity-shop chains. Below them are one-room foodbanks, community-centre pantries and volunteer-run projects working on a shoestring across Bangor, Coed Mawr and Maesgeirchen. Our aim is to serve the national charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts AND direct online ordering, no minimum, so cost never stops a small group getting kitted out.

Bangor's voluntary life leans on its volunteer centre and student energy. Mantell Gwynedd runs the county Volunteer Centre, advising small community and voluntary groups and brokering placements, while Undeb Bangor, the students' union, channels volunteers into local projects through its Big Give scheme. Hope House and Cancer Research shops on the High Street raise money for hospice and cancer care. Chapel congregations, community-centre teams at Coed Mawr and Maesgeirchen, and residents' groups draw out steady helpers, and seasonal collections and warm-space sessions keep the city's smaller projects ticking over.
